title: Venus et Mars. Leucothoe. Clytie
titleEn: Venus and Mars; the Sun, Leucothoe and Clytie — Metamorphoses IV.167–270
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Leuconoe, the next of the daughters of Minyas to take her turn at the telling, tells two linked tales about the Sun. First, how the god who sees everything saw it first when Venus went to bed with Mars, and told her husband Vulcan, who forged a net of bronze too fine for the eye, caught the pair in it, and threw the doors open to the laughing gods. Venus takes her revenge by making the Sun himself fall in love: he neglects the sky for a Persian girl, Leucothoe, and both she and the jealous nymph Clytie are destroyed by it — the one becoming the frankincense shrub, the other the flower that turns after the sun all day. The Latin is dactylic hexameter, and Ovid's sentences run freely across the verse lines, so the unit you tap often begins or ends in mid-line; the line numbers are the standard way to cite the poem.

advisory.lede: This part contains a rape: the Sun enters Leucothoe's bedchamber disguised as her mother and takes her by force, and her father buries her alive when he learns of it.
advisory.more: Ovid gives the act half a line — posita vim passa querella est, "her protest laid aside, she suffered his force" — in language decorous enough that a reader can pass over it. Vim pati was the plain Latin phrase for being raped, the one the courts used, and the poem does not blur what it means: the girl is called terrified and overcome in the same line, and six lines later, pleading with her father, she says it herself, ille vim tulit invitae, "he forced me, unwilling." She is telling the truth and is buried alive for it, and the punishment falls on her rather than on the god, who is left to grieve and to make her into incense. The tale is told as an afternoon's entertainment by one of the daughters of Minyas, and neither she nor the poem stops to judge it. Lectorium presents the text as it was written, unaltered; the notes say plainly what the Latin says, and where it is being decorous about it.

sentences.t:
Desierat, mediumque fuit breve tempus, et orsa est
dicere Leuconoe: vocem tenuere sorores.
sentences.l:
She had ceased, and the time between was brief, and Leuconoe
began to speak: her sisters held their voices.
sentences.i: She had finished, and after a short pause Leuconoe began to speak; her sisters fell silent.
sentences.n: 'Desierat' is a pluperfect standing alone: the sister who told of Pyramus and Thisbe has just stopped. These are the daughters of Minyas, who stayed at their looms telling stories rather than join the rites of Bacchus. 'orsa est' (deponent perfect of ordior) is 'made a beginning.' 'vocem tenuere sorores' is literally 'the sisters held their voice' — they kept silent. And 'tenuere' = 'tenuerunt': the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ēre, which runs all through this poem (venere, iacuere, risere, cecidere all follow below). Flagging it once here; after this it is only a nudge.

sentences.t:
“Hunc quoque, siderea qui temperat omnia luce,
cepit amor Solem: Solis referemus amores.
sentences.l:
Him too — the one who regulates all things with his starry light —
love took, the Sun: the Sun's loves we shall relate.
sentences.i: Love took him too, the Sun, who keeps all things in their due measure with his starry light; and it is the Sun's love-affairs I shall tell.
sentences.n: The object comes first and is held apart from its own noun: 'Hunc… Solem' ('him… the Sun') with the relative clause set between them, a favourite Ovidian arrangement. 'temperat' is not 'tempers' in the English sense but 'keeps in due measure, regulates' — the Sun as the ordering power of the world, which is exactly the office love is about to spoil. 'referemus' is a plural of the single speaker; 'amores' in the plural regularly means love-affairs.

sentences.t:
Primus adulterium Veneris cum Marte putatur
hic vidisse deus: videt hic deus omnia primus.
sentences.l:
First to have seen the adultery of Venus with Mars, this god
is thought: this god sees all things first.
sentences.i: This god is thought to have been the first to see Venus's adultery with Mars — as he is first to see everything.
sentences.n: 'putatur… vidisse' is the personal passive of putare with an infinitive: 'he is thought to have seen,' where English prefers 'it is thought that he saw.' The point is in the repetition — 'primus' opening one line and closing the next, with 'hic deus' repeated between them: the Sun sees first not by luck but by definition. 'adulterium' is the flat legal word for the offence, and Venus is the wife of Vulcan.

sentences.t:
Indoluit facto, Iunonigenaeque marito
furta tori furtique locum monstravit.
sentences.l:
He grieved at the deed, and to the Juno-born husband
he showed the bed's thefts and the theft's place.
sentences.i: He was pained at the deed, and showed Juno's son, the husband, the stolen love and where it was stolen.
sentences.n: 'Iunonigenae' — 'Juno-born,' a compound made for the line: Vulcan, whom Juno bore, and whose whole standing in this story is 'the husband' ('marito', dative with 'monstravit'). 'furta tori' ('the thefts of the bed') is the ordinary Latin idiom for a secret affair; Ovid then reuses the word with hard literalness in 'furtique locum,' the place where the theft was done. 'facto' is an ablative of cause.

sentences.t:
At illi
et mens et quod opus fabrilis dextra tenebat
excidit.
sentences.l:
But from him both his mind and the work which his smith's right hand
was holding fell away.
sentences.i: But his wits dropped out of him, and so did the work his smith's right hand was holding.
sentences.n: 'illi' is a dative of the person affected: things fall 'for him,' which English turns into 'from him.' 'excidit' (slipped, fell out) is singular though it governs two subjects, 'mens' and 'opus,' and carries both at once — his wits and his tools go together, which is the joke. 'fabrilis dextra,' the craftsman's right hand, names Vulcan by the only part of him that matters here.

sentences.t:
Extemplo graciles ex aere catenas
retiaque et laqueos, quae lumina fallere possent,
elimat
sentences.l:
At once slender chains of bronze
and nets and nooses, such as could cheat the eyes,
he files out.
sentences.i: At once he files out slender chains of bronze, and nets and snares fine enough to escape the eye.
sentences.n: The verb is held back to the head of the third line: 'elimat,' 'files smooth, files out' — the smith's own word, with the whole apparatus hanging in the air waiting for it. 'quae… possent' is a relative clause of characteristic (subjunctive): 'of a kind that could cheat the eyes.' 'lumina' is 'lights' and so 'eyes' — watch that word, it will be used of the Sun's own eyes, of lamplight, and of daylight before this part is over.

sentences.t:
(non illud opus tenuissima vincant
stamina, non summo quae pendet aranea tigno),
sentences.l:
(that work the finest threads could not outdo,
nor the spider that hangs from the topmost beam),
sentences.i: (the finest thread could not better that work, nor the spider hanging from the highest rafter),
sentences.n: A parenthesis breaking into the middle of the making. The aside belongs to the narrator, and the narrator here is Leuconoe, who has been speaking since 169 — these asides sound like Ovid's own, but the poem has put them in her mouth. 'vincant' is a potential subjunctive, 'could not outdo.' The comparison reaches for the proverbial limit of fineness: not a metaphorical web but 'aranea,' the spider herself, hanging where a real one hangs, from the roof-beam ('summo tigno').

sentences.t:
utque leves tactus momentaque parva sequantur
efficit et lecto circumdata collocat arte.
sentences.l:
and he brings it about that they answer light touches and slight movements,
and he sets them, ranged about the bed, with art.
sentences.i: and he contrives that they answer to the lightest touch, the least movement, and arranges them skilfully all around the bed.
sentences.n: 'efficit ut… sequantur' — 'he brings it about that they follow' — is a result clause, and it is the language of a trap set to a hair-trigger. 'momenta' are literally 'movements,' the small shiftings of a weight (from moveo). 'circumdata' is neuter plural agreeing with the nets and chains, 'placed around'; 'arte' closes the line as an ablative of manner — and it is the same word that opens the trap's springing two lines on, at 183.

sentences.t:
Ut venere torum coniunx et adulter in unum,
arte viri vinclisque nova ratione paratis
in mediis ambo deprensi amplexibus haerent.
sentences.l:
When wife and adulterer came into one bed together,
by the husband's art and by bonds prepared on a new plan
both, caught in the midst of their embraces, hang fast.
sentences.i: When wife and adulterer came together into the one bed, the husband's art and his newly contrived bonds caught them both, and they hung there fast in mid-embrace.
sentences.n: 'venere' = 'venerunt' — the -ēre perfect again, as promised. 'coniunx' here is the wife, Venus; 'adulter' names Mars by nothing but his offence. 'in mediis… amplexibus' is 'in the middle of their embraces,' the Latin for 'in the very act,' and 'haerent' is a present tense that leaves them stuck there in front of us. Note 'arte' picked up from 181, two lines back: the art that made the net is the art that springs it.

sentences.i: The Lemnian flung the ivory doors wide at once and let the gods in; and there the two lay bound, in their shame.
sentences.n: 'Lemnius' — 'the Lemnian': Vulcan, named from Lemnos, the island where he was said to have fallen and to keep his forge. Naming a god by his place is standard here, and 'Hyperione nate' will do the same for the Sun a few lines on. 'iacuere' is another -ēre perfect. 'turpiter' is thrown alone into the next line, so the shame lands after the sentence looks finished. Some editions read 'inmisitque' for Magnus's 'admisitque'; the sense barely shifts.

sentences.t:
atque aliquis de dis non tristibus optat
sic fieri turpis:
sentences.l:
and one of the gods — the ones who are not solemn — prays
to be made shameful in just that way:
sentences.i: and one of the less solemn gods prays that he might be shamed like that.
sentences.n: 'de dis non tristibus' is a litotes — 'from among the gods who are not grim,' saying 'not solemn' where it means 'cheerful' — and it leaves the god politely unnamed ('aliquis,' someone). 'sic fieri turpis' is 'to become disgraced in that fashion': the wish is to be caught in exactly that position. Ovid puts the joke in the mouth of a nobody so that nobody has to answer for it.

sentences.t:
superi risere, diuque
haec fuit in toto notissima fabula caelo.
sentences.l:
the gods above laughed, and long
this was the best-known story in the whole of heaven.
sentences.i: The gods above laughed, and for a long time this was the most talked-of story in all heaven.
sentences.n: 'risere' = 'riserunt': the -ēre perfect once more. 'fabula' is both 'story' and 'the talk' — what everyone is telling. The line is a closing formula, and its content is the point: the affair ends not in punishment but in gossip, which is this poem's usual measure of Olympus.

sentences.t:
Exigit indicii memorem Cythereia poenam,
inque vices illum, tectos qui laesit amores,
laedit amore pari.
sentences.l:
The Cytherean exacts a penalty that remembers the informing,
and in turn him, who wounded her hidden loves,
she wounds with a love to match.
sentences.i: Venus exacts a punishment that does not forget the denunciation: him who wounded her hidden love she wounds in turn, with a love of the same kind.
sentences.n: 'Cythereia' is Venus, named from Cythera, the island off which she was said to have risen. 'poenam memorem indicii' is 'a punishment mindful of the informing' — the adjective does the remembering, a transfer English has to unpick. The revenge is built out of one verb turned back on itself, 'laesit… laedit' (he wounded… she wounds), and 'amores… amore' does the same. 'in vices' = 'by turns, in exchange.'

sentences.t:
Quid nunc, Hyperione nate,
forma colorque tibi radiataque lumina prosunt?
sentences.l:
What now, son of Hyperion,
do beauty and colour and your rayed eyes profit you?
sentences.i: What good to you now, child of Hyperion, are your beauty, your colour, your radiant eyes?
sentences.n: The narrator turns from the story to speak to the Sun himself. This is apostrophe — the teller stepping aside to address a character — and he reaches for it whenever he wants the reader to pity or accuse; it runs in the second person for the next dozen lines and comes back for Leucothoe at 242. 'Hyperione nate' is a vocative, 'O son of Hyperion,' the Titan father of the Sun. 'prosunt' (from prosum) takes the dative 'tibi,' 'are of use to you.' 'lumina' again: his lights are both his eyes and his rays. 'color' is his complexion, and the word comes back at 203, when love has changed what colour that is.

sentences.t:
Nempe tuis omnes qui terras ignibus uris,
ureris igne novo;
sentences.l:
You, surely, who burn all lands with fires of your own,
are burned by a fire that is new;
sentences.i: You who scorch every land with your own fire are scorched yourself by a fire that is new to you;
sentences.n: One verb in two voices carries the whole line: 'uris' (you burn, active) answered by 'ureris' (you are burned, passive) at the head of the next. Burning is the standing Latin metaphor for being in love, and here it is metaphor and literal fact at once. 'nempe' is a dry particle — 'of course, naturally' — with a distinct edge of 'so much for that.'

sentences.t:
quique omnia cernere debes,
Leucothoen spectas, et virgine figis in una,
quos mundo debes oculos.
sentences.l:
and you who ought to look upon all things
gaze at Leucothoe, and you fasten upon one girl
the eyes you owe the world.
sentences.i: and you, whose office is to see everything, stare at Leucothoe, and fix on a single girl the eyes you owe the whole world.
sentences.n: 'debes' is used twice in two senses that Latin keeps in one word and English has to split: 'you ought to see' and 'the eyes you owe.' The Sun's obligation and his debt are the same thing. 'Leucothoen' keeps its Greek accusative, as Greek names regularly do in this poem. And note where the sentence ends: 'oculos' comes last of all, after the relative clause that describes it, so we learn only at the close what it is he is misusing.

sentences.t:
Modo surgis Eoo
temperius caelo, modo serius incidis undis,
spectandique mora brumales porrigis horas,
sentences.l:
Now you rise too early in the eastern sky,
now too late you fall into the waves,
and by the delay of gazing you draw out the winter hours,
sentences.i: Now you rise too early in the eastern sky, now you sink too late into the sea; and lingering to look, you draw out even the short hours of winter.
sentences.n: 'temperius' is the comparative of 'tempori' ('in good time'), so 'earlier than he should'; 'serius' is the comparative of 'sero,' later. 'Eoo caelo' is the eastern sky, from Greek Eos, dawn. 'spectandi mora' — 'by the delay of gazing,' a gerund in the genitive — says he is late because he is looking. 'brumales horas' are the hours of midwinter, proverbially the shortest, and love is stretching even those. The astronomy is the argument: a god in love makes the day itself unreliable.

sentences.t:
deficis interdum, vitiumque in lumina mentis
transit et obscurus mortalia pectora terres.
sentences.l:
sometimes you fail, and the mind's flaw
passes over into your light, and darkened you terrify mortal hearts.
sentences.i: sometimes you go out altogether, and the sickness of your mind passes into your light, and darkened, you terrify the hearts of men.
sentences.n: 'deficis' is the standing verb for an eclipse: the Sun 'fails.' Ovid's explanation is that an eclipse is love-sickness made visible — 'vitium mentis,' the mind's defect, crosses over ('transit') into the 'lumina.' 'obscurus' is a predicate adjective doing adverbial work, 'you, being darkened, terrify'; Latin verse reaches for an adjective where English wants an adverb or a clause, and you will meet it constantly.

sentences.t:
Nec, tibi quod lunae terris propioris imago
obstiterit, palles: facit hunc amor iste colorem.
sentences.l:
Nor is it because the disc of the moon, nearer to the earth,
has stood in your way that you are pale: that love of yours makes this colour.
sentences.i: And your paleness is not because the moon, which rides nearer the earth, has come between: it is that love of yours that gives you this colour.
sentences.n: The 'quod' clause is what the sentence denies, not what it asserts: 'it is not because the moon blocked you that you are pale.' The correct physical account of an eclipse is given and then set aside in favour of the poem's. 'imago' is the moon's shape or disc; 'propioris' (nearer) is the ordinary ancient view, the moon being lowest of the heavenly bodies. 'iste' is never quite neutral — 'that love of yours,' with a shade of reproach in it.

sentences.t:
Diligis hanc unam; nec te Clymeneque Rhodosque
nec tenet Aeaeae genetrix pulcherrima Circes,
sentences.l:
You love this one alone; and neither Clymene nor Rhodos
holds you, nor the most beautiful mother of Aeaean Circe,
sentences.i: You love this one girl alone: Clymene no longer holds you, nor Rhodos, nor the lovely mother of Circe of Aeaea,
sentences.n: Three earlier loves of the Sun, dropped in without explanation because a Roman reader had them by heart: Clymene, mother of Phaethon (Book II); Rhodos, the nymph of the island of Rhodes; and the mother of Circe, called Perse in the usual account and named here only as somebody's mother — Ovid's habit when the daughter is the more famous. 'Aeaeae' is an adjective agreeing with 'Circes' — Circe of Aeaea, the island she lives on. 'tenet' is singular though it has three subjects, agreeing with the nearest, which is normal.

sentences.t:
quaeque tuos Clytie quamvis despecta petebat
concubitus ipsoque illo grave vulnus habebat
tempore:
sentences.l:
and Clytie, who, though scorned, kept seeking your
bed, and at that very time was carrying a heavy wound:
sentences.i: nor Clytie, who went on seeking your bed though you scorned her, and at that very moment was nursing a deep wound:
sentences.n: 'quaeque' is 'and she who': the relative carries the subject of 'tenet' forward from the line before, with Clytie's own name set inside her clause. 'despecta' (looked down on, scorned) works concessively with 'quamvis.' 'concubitus' is plural in form and blunt in sense, the act of going to bed. 'grave vulnus' is the wound of love, the standard metaphor, and it is this wound that drives the second half of the tale. 'ipso illo… tempore' is split around the line-end: 'at that very time,' meaning while he was already turning away.

sentences.t:
Leucothoe multarum oblivia fecit,
gentis odoriferae quam formosissima partu
edidit Eurynome.
sentences.l:
Leucothoe made a forgetting of many women,
whom Eurynome, most beautiful of the fragrance-bearing nation,
brought forth in childbirth.
sentences.i: Leucothoe made him forget them all — Leucothoe, whom Eurynome, the loveliest woman of that perfumed nation, bore.
sentences.n: 'oblivia fecit' is 'made forgettings,' an abstract plural for 'made him forget,' with 'multarum' genitive feminine, 'of many women.' 'gentis odoriferae' is the frankincense country, Arabia, named by its scent instead of its name — which is quiet preparation for what the girl becomes. 'partu edidit' is the ordinary phrase for giving birth, 'brought forth by a bearing.' The word order is at its most Ovidian: 'quam' sits in the middle of its own clause, wedged between the genitive and the superlative that belong together.

sentences.t:
Sed postquam filia crevit,
quam mater cunctas, tam matrem filia vicit.
sentences.l:
But after the daughter grew,
by as much as the mother outdid all women, by so much the daughter outdid the mother.
sentences.i: But once the daughter was grown, she surpassed her mother by just as much as her mother had surpassed all other women.
sentences.n: 'quam… tam' is the correlative pair — 'by however much… by that much' — with one verb, 'vicit,' serving both halves; Latin can leave the first verb out where English cannot. The line is built as a crossing: mother / all women, then mother / daughter, so that 'matrem filia' stand side by side at the end where the point is. It is a formula of praise, used here to make the god's attention feel inevitable.

sentences.t:
Rexit Achaemenias urbes pater Orchamus, isque
septimus a prisco numeratur origine Belo.
sentences.l:
Her father Orchamus ruled Achaemenian cities, and he
is counted seventh from ancient Belus in descent.
sentences.i: Her father Orchamus ruled the cities of Persia, and is reckoned seventh in line from ancient Belus.
sentences.n: 'Achaemenias' means Achaemenid, that is Persian, using the name of the historical Persian royal house for a legendary East — the anachronism is deliberate and gives the story a real address. Belus is the founding eastern king of Greek genealogy. 'numeratur septimus a… Belo' is the Roman way of stating a descent, counting outward from the ancestor rather than back from the descendant.

sentences.t: Axe sub Hesperio sunt pascua Solis equorum.
sentences.l: Beneath the western pole are the pastures of the Sun's horses.
sentences.i: Under the western sky lie the pastures of the Sun's horses.
sentences.n: 'axis' is the axle of the sky and so, by extension, the sky itself or one quarter of it; 'Hesperio' is 'of the evening, western,' from Greek Hesperos. The pastures are where the team goes at the end of the day's drive. The mythology is stated as plain geography, in one line that stands entirely alone — and this quiet paragraph is how Ovid gets the god off duty and into the girl's house.

sentences.t:
Ambrosiam pro gramine habent: ea fessa diurnis
membra ministeriis nutrit reparatque labori.
sentences.l:
They have ambrosia in place of grass: it feeds their limbs,
wearied by the day's service, and restores them for their labour.
sentences.i: They graze on ambrosia instead of grass; it feeds their limbs, worn out by the day's work, and makes them fit for labour again.
sentences.n: 'ea' is feminine singular, picking up 'ambrosiam' as the subject of 'nutrit'; it can also be read as neuter plural with 'membra' ('those limbs'), which leaves the sense unchanged. 'fessa… membra' (wearied limbs) is pulled apart across the line-end with 'diurnis ministeriis' set between them, a normal Latin way of packing an image tight. 'ministerium' is service, the word for a servant's round of duties: the immortal horses are on shift. 'labori' is a dative of purpose, restores them 'for the work' still to come.

sentences.t:
Dumque ibi quadrupedes caelestia pabula carpunt,
noxque vicem peragit, thalamos deus intrat amatos,
versus in Eurynomes faciem genetricis,
sentences.l:
And while the four-footed ones there crop the heavenly fodder
and night runs its turn through, the god enters the longed-for bedchamber,
turned into the face of her mother Eurynome,
sentences.i: And while the horses crop their heavenly fodder there and night takes its turn, the god enters the bedchamber he wants, changed into the shape of her mother Eurynome,
sentences.n: 'dum' with a present indicative for one action going on while another happens. 'quadrupedes' — 'four-footed ones' — is the epic way of naming horses without naming them. 'vicem peragit' is 'carries its turn through': night has a shift as the horses do. 'thalamos amatos' is a plural for a singular, common in verse, and the loving in 'amatos' is his, not hers. 'versus in… faciem' — 'turned into the face of' — makes the disguise the god's first move, and it is her mother's face he takes. 'Eurynomes' keeps its Greek genitive ending.

sentences.t:
et inter
bis sex Leucothoen famulas ad lumina cernit
levia versato ducentem stamina fuso.
sentences.l:
and among
twice six handmaids he makes out Leucothoe by the lights,
drawing out smooth threads with the twirled spindle.
sentences.i: and there among twelve handmaids he makes out Leucothoe by lamplight, drawing smooth thread from a turning spindle.
sentences.n: 'bis sex' — twice six for twelve: verse prefers the figure to the plain numeral. 'ad lumina' is 'by the lights,' the lamps of the room — that word again, and here it belongs to the household rather than to the god. 'versato… fuso' is an ablative absolute in miniature, 'the spindle having been twirled,' which English turns into 'with a turning spindle.' Spinning is the standing sign of a virtuous woman indoors — and it is exactly what the daughters of Minyas are doing while they tell this story.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi ceu mater carae dedit oscula natae,
“res” ait “arcana est.
sentences.l:
So when, as a mother would, he gave kisses to the dear daughter,
"the matter," he says, "is a secret one.
sentences.i: So, when he had kissed the dear girl as a mother does, he said: "This is a secret matter.
sentences.n: 'ceu' is 'just as,' a poetic word, and it holds the disguise up to view: he kisses her the way a mother kisses. 'carae natae' is dative with 'dedit oscula,' and 'nata' ('daughter,' literally 'the one born') is the mother's own word, part of the impersonation. 'ait' is a defective verb used almost only for speech, and it is dropped in among the quoted words rather than set before them — Latin verse marks direct speech by wrapping the tag inside it.

sentences.t:
Famulae, discedite neve
eripite arbitrium matri secreta loquendi.”
sentences.l:
Handmaids, withdraw, and do not
snatch from a mother the freedom of speaking secrets."
sentences.i: Handmaids, leave us, and do not rob a mother of the right to speak her secrets."
sentences.n: 'neve… eripite' joins a negative command to the imperative before it: 'and do not.' 'arbitrium… loquendi' is 'the free decision of speaking,' a gerund in the genitive; 'matri' is a dative of separation, 'from a mother.' The god borrows a mother's authority to clear the room, and the reader watches a trap being laid in language of unimpeachable propriety.

sentences.t:
Paruerant: thalamoque deus sine teste relicto
“ille ego sum” dixit, “qui longum metior annum,
sentences.l:
They had obeyed: and the chamber left without a witness,
the god said, "I am he who measures out the long year,
sentences.i: They obeyed; and with the room left without a witness, the god said: "I am the one who measures out the long year,
sentences.n: 'Paruerant' is a pluperfect standing as a whole sentence — 'they had obeyed' — already done before we are told of it, which is how fast the room empties. 'thalamo sine teste relicto' is an ablative absolute: a self-contained 'with the chamber left witnessless' where English wants a clause ('once the room had been left…'). This construction is everywhere in Latin verse; flagging it here, and you will meet three more before this part ends. 'ille ego sum qui…' is the formula of a god declaring himself, the relative clauses doing the work a name would do.

sentences.t:
omnia qui video, per quem videt omnia tellus,
mundi oculus.
sentences.l:
who see all things, through whom the earth sees all things,
the eye of the world.
sentences.i: who see everything, through whom the earth sees everything — the eye of the world.
sentences.n: Two relative clauses hang on the same 'ille,' and then the phrase they have been building toward stands alone at the head of the line: 'mundi oculus,' the eye of the world. The boast is exactly what the poem has already turned against him — the god who sees everything was made a spy in the first paragraph, and is now announcing the fact to a girl he has come to in a stolen shape.

sentences.t:
Mihi, crede, places.” Pavet illa, metuque
et colus et fusus digitis cecidere remissis.
sentences.l:
Believe me: you please me." She is in terror, and out of fear
both distaff and spindle fell from her slackened fingers.
sentences.i: Believe me — you please me." She was terrified, and in her fear both distaff and spindle dropped from her loosened fingers.
sentences.n: 'places' is the plain verb 'you are pleasing,' with the dative 'mihi': the declaration is three words long. 'Pavet' is a historic present dropped in among perfects, putting her fear in front of us as it happens; 'cecidere' is the -ēre perfect again. 'digitis remissis' is another ablative absolute, 'her fingers having gone slack.' The spinning of two lines ago comes undone in half a line, and the image carries what she feels without a word of statement.

sentences.t:
Ipse timor decuit. Nec longius ille moratus
in veram rediit speciem solitumque nitorem:
sentences.l:
Fear itself became her. And he, delaying no longer,
went back into his true shape and his accustomed brilliance:
sentences.i: Her very fear became her. And he, waiting no longer, returned to his true form and his usual brilliance.
sentences.n: 'decet' is the verb of what suits or looks well on a person, so 'Ipse timor decuit' is 'her fear itself was becoming to her.' Three words, and among the coldest in the poem: it is the narrator, not the god, who stops to appraise her terror as something that suits her. 'moratus' is the deponent participle of 'moror,' passive in form and active in sense. 'nitor' is the shine of a polished surface, the ordinary word for a god's radiance.

sentences.t:
at virgo, quamvis inopino territa visu,
victa nitore dei posita vim passa querella est.
sentences.l:
but the girl, though terrified by the unlooked-for sight,
overcome by the god's brilliance, her protest laid down, suffered his force.
sentences.i: But the girl, terrified as she was by the sudden sight, was overborne by the god's brilliance, and with her protest given up she endured his violence.
sentences.n: 'vim passa est' — 'she suffered force' — is the settled Latin phrase for being raped; it is what the courts said, and the decorum of the surrounding words does not soften it. 'posita querella' is an ablative absolute, 'her complaint having been laid aside': the protest stops, which is not the same thing as consent, and the line keeps 'territa' (terrified) and 'victa' (beaten, overcome) standing in front of it. Both participles are passive — everything she does in this sentence is done to her. Her own account comes at line 239 and says it flatly: 'ille vim tulit invitae,' he forced me, unwilling.

sentences.t:
Invidit Clytie (neque enim moderatus in illa
Solis amor fuerat),
sentences.l:
Clytie was jealous (for the Sun's love toward her
had not been a measured one),
sentences.i: Clytie was jealous — the Sun's love for her had been no measured thing —
sentences.n: 'Invidit' is 'looked upon with envy.' The parenthesis explains her jealousy out of the past, with 'in illa' meaning 'in her case, toward her.' 'moderatus' — kept within measure — is the same idea of proportion that governs the Sun's whole office and that this part keeps testing against his loves; 'moderator' will be used of him as driver at 245. The bracket is the poet excusing her a moment before she does the thing he will not excuse.

sentences.t:
stimulataque paelicis ira
vulgat adulterium diffamatumque parenti
indicat.
sentences.l:
and goaded by anger at the rival mistress
she spreads the adultery abroad and, once it was notorious, to the father
she reveals it.
sentences.i: and, goaded by anger at the rival mistress, she spread the adultery abroad, and once it was notorious she told the girl's father.
sentences.n: 'paelicis ira' can be read two ways, and the choice matters: the anger of a rival mistress, meaning Clytie's own as the supplanted woman, or anger directed at the rival, meaning Leucothoe. We take the second. 'paelex' is not a neutral status word — it is the contemptuous term for the other woman in a man's bed — and it is Clytie's view of Leucothoe, not the poem's: Leucothoe was taken by force two lines earlier. 'diffamatum' is neuter, agreeing with 'adulterium': the rumour is spread first, the denunciation comes after. Some editions read 'diffamatamque,' which makes the girl herself the one who has been made notorious.

sentences.t:
Ille ferox inmansuetusque precantem
tendentemque manus ad lumina Solis et “ille
vim tulit invitae” dicentem defodit alta
crudus humo, tumulumque super gravis addit harenae.
sentences.l:
He, fierce and untamed, as she begged
and stretched her hands toward the Sun's light and said
"he forced me, unwilling" — buried her deep
in the earth, pitiless, and heaps a mound of heavy sand above.
sentences.i: Her father, fierce and unrelenting, while she begged and stretched her hands out toward the Sun's light and cried "he took me by force, against my will" — buried her, pitiless, deep in the earth, and heaped a mound of heavy sand on top.
sentences.n: Three participles in a row — 'precantem, tendentem, dicentem' — all agree with her, the object, and hold the sentence open across three lines while the main verb 'defodit' (buries) is kept waiting: the delay is the sentence enacting what it describes. 'vim tulit invitae' is her own account and it answers the poem's own phrase at 233; 'vim ferre' is to inflict force, and 'invitae' is a dative, 'upon her, unwilling.' She tells the truth and is buried alive for it. 'crudus' is 'raw, unsoftened,' and of a man, pitiless. 'gravis' goes with 'harenae' — a mound of heavy sand, and that weight is what kills her at 243. The poem passes no judgement on the father: what follows is the Sun's grief, not justice.

sentences.t:
Dissipat hunc radiis Hyperione natus iterque
dat tibi, qua possis defossos promere vultus.
sentences.l:
The son of Hyperion scatters this with his rays, and gives
you a way, by which you might bring out your buried face.
sentences.i: The son of Hyperion scattered the mound with his rays and gave you an opening by which to bring your buried face out.
sentences.n: The apostrophe comes back, and this time it is the girl who is addressed: 'iter dat tibi,' 'he gives you a road.' Ovid turns to a character in the second person at the moment nothing can be done for her — the same move he made for the Sun at 192, now used for pity instead of accusation. 'qua' is adverbial, 'by which way,' with 'possis' subjunctive of purpose. 'vultus' is a plural for a singular, ordinary in verse.

sentences.t:
Nec tu iam poteras enectum pondere terrae
tollere, nympha, caput corpusque exsangue iacebas.
sentences.l:
But you could no longer lift your head, killed
by the weight of the earth, nymph, and you lay a bloodless body.
sentences.i: But you could no longer lift your head, crushed dead by the weight of the earth, nymph; you lay there, a body without blood.
sentences.n: 'enectum' ('killed off, done to death') belongs to 'caput,' which is held back into the next line, so the participle hangs unattached for a whole line before we learn what it describes. 'corpus exsangue' stands in apposition to the subject 'tu': 'you lay, a bloodless body.' 'exsanguis' is the standard word for a corpse — and it will come back at 267, transferred to leaves. The vocative 'nympha' set inside the line keeps the poet speaking to her at the moment she stops being able to answer. 'nympha' is used loosely here for a girl — Leucothoe is a king's daughter, not a nymph; Clytie, called the same thing at 260, is one in the usual account.

sentences.t:
Nil illo fertur volucrum moderator equorum
post Phaethonteos vidisse dolentius ignes.
sentences.l:
Nothing more grievous than that, they say, did the driver of the winged horses
see after the fires of Phaethon.
sentences.i: The driver of the winged horses is said to have seen nothing more painful than this since Phaethon's fires.
sentences.n: 'moderator equorum' — 'the controller of the horses' — is the Sun by his office rather than his name, and 'moderator' comes from the same root as 'moderatus' at 234: the god whose whole business is keeping things in measure. 'fertur… vidisse' is the personal passive again, 'he is said to have seen.' 'illo… dolentius' is an ablative of comparison. Phaethon's fires are the catastrophe of Book II, when the Sun's son took the chariot and burned the world — that is the scale being invoked for one girl's death.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem gelidos radiorum viribus artus
si queat in vivum temptat revocare calorem:
sentences.l:
He indeed tries, if he should be able, with the strength of his rays
to call her cold limbs back into living warmth:
sentences.i: He does try, if he can, to call her cold limbs back to living warmth by the force of his rays;
sentences.n: 'gelidos… artus' (cold limbs) is stretched around the whole line, with the conditional 'si queat' ('in case he can,' potential subjunctive) tucked inside the main clause rather than in front of it. 'in vivum calorem' is 'into living heat,' where the calling-back is aimed. Everything the Sun has is warmth and light, and here neither one is any use — the line is arranged so that the effort surrounds a body it cannot reach.

sentences.t:
sed quoniam tantis fatum conatibus obstat,
nectare odorato sparsit corpusque locumque,
sentences.l:
but since fate stands against efforts even so great,
he sprinkled with fragrant nectar both the body and the place,
sentences.i: but since fate blocks efforts even as great as his, he sprinkled fragrant nectar over the body and the place alike,
sentences.n: 'obstat' takes the dative 'conatibus': fate 'stands in the way for' his attempts. That even the Sun is under fate is stated flatly and never argued in this poem. The doubled '-que… -que' joining 'corpus' and 'locum' is the epic connective, 'both… and.' 'nectare odorato,' the scented drink of the gods, is the first hint of what will grow in that place.

sentences.t: multaque praequestus “tanges tamen aethera” dixit.
sentences.l: and having first lamented much, he said, "yet you shall touch the upper air."
sentences.i: and after much lamenting he said: "Even so, you shall reach the sky."
sentences.n: 'praequestus' is a rare compound — 'having complained beforehand,' prae- with queror, a deponent participle active in sense — and it may well be Ovid's own coinage. 'multa' is an internal accusative, 'lamented many things.' The promise is deliberately double-edged: she will touch the sky, but as incense-smoke rising from an altar, and not otherwise. 'aethera' is a Greek accusative singular.

sentences.t:
Protinus inbutum caelesti nectare corpus
dilicuit terramque suo madefecit odore:
sentences.l:
At once the body, steeped in heavenly nectar,
melted away and drenched the earth with a fragrance of its own:
sentences.i: At once the body, soaked with heavenly nectar, melted away and drenched the earth with its scent;
sentences.n: 'inbutum' keeps Magnus's unassimilated spelling where other editions print 'imb-'; this edition's orthography is preserved throughout, and 'inmansuetus' at 237 stood on the same principle. 'dilicuit' is from deliquesco, 'to melt away, dissolve.' Note what kind of transformation this is: a dissolving, not a reshaping. What is left of her is a smell in the ground, and the plant grows out of that.

sentences.t:
virgaque per glaebas sensim radicibus actis
turea surrexit tumulumque cacumine rupit.
sentences.l:
and a shoot, its roots driven little by little through the clods,
a frankincense shoot rose up and broke the mound open with its tip.
sentences.i: and a shoot of frankincense, its roots pushing slowly through the clods, rose and broke the mound open with its tip.
sentences.n: 'radicibus actis' is another ablative absolute — 'the roots having been driven' — with 'sensim' (little by little) set inside it, which is how the slowness gets into the sentence. 'virga… turea' is split across the line-end so that 'turea' lands first in its own line and names the plant only at the last moment: this is why her mother was 'of the fragrance-bearing nation' back at 209. The incense that rises from every Roman altar is what she becomes, which is exactly how the god's promise is kept and how little it is worth.

sentences.t:
At Clytien, quamvis amor excusare dolorem,
indiciumque dolor poterat, non amplius auctor
lucis adit venerisque modum sibi fecit in illa.
sentences.l:
But Clytie — though love could excuse her grief,
and grief her informing — the author of light
approached no more, and made for himself an end of love in her case.
sentences.i: But the author of light came to Clytie no more, though love might excuse her grief and grief excuse her denunciation, and he put an end in himself to all love of her.
sentences.n: The concessions are stacked in a chain: love excuses grief, grief excuses the denunciation. The sentence grants both and refuses her anyway, which is the whole of her judgement in two lines. 'auctor lucis' — 'the maker of light' — is the Sun again by office rather than name. 'venerisque modum sibi fecit in illa' is compressed: 'he made himself a limit of love in her case,' meaning he was finished with her. 'venus' with a small letter is the act and the appetite, not the goddess. 'Clytien' is a Greek accusative.

sentences.t:
Tabuit ex illo dementer amoribus usa
nympha larum inpatiens,
sentences.l:
From that time she wasted away, a nymph who had used her love madly,
unable to bear a roof,
sentences.i: From that day she pined away, a nymph who had spent her love in madness and could not endure to be indoors,
sentences.n: 'tabuit' (from tabesco) is the verb of a body melting or wasting, and it will end by being literally true. 'amoribus usa' is 'having made use of her loves,' with 'dementer' — out of her mind — as the poem's verdict on how. Magnus prints 'nympha larum inpatiens,' 'the nymph unable to bear the household gods,' that is, unable to stay under a roof; other editions read 'nympharum inpatiens,' unable to bear the company of the other nymphs. Magnus's reading is the one the next lines support, since she sits out of doors for nine days.

sentences.t:
et sub Iove nocte dieque
sedit humo nuda, nudis incompta capillis,
sentences.l:
and under Jupiter, by night and by day,
she sat on the bare ground, uncombed, her hair uncovered,
sentences.i: and under the open sky, night and day, she sat on the bare ground, uncombed, her hair uncovered,
sentences.n: 'sub Iove' is 'under Jupiter' and so 'in the open air' — the god's name standing for the sky he rules, which Latin does constantly. 'humo nuda' is ablative and the bareness is the ground's, though the word sits close enough to her to shadow the other reading. 'nudis capillis' means the hair is uncovered, without the band or veil a respectable woman wore outdoors; with 'incompta' (uncombed) it is the standard picture of mourning. Note the repetition straddling the middle of the line: 'nuda… nudis.'

sentences.t:
perque novem luces expers undaeque cibique
rore mero lacrimisque suis ieiunia pavit
nec se movit humo:
sentences.l:
and through nine daylights, having no share of water or of food,
on unmixed dew and on her own tears she fed her fastings,
and did not move herself from the ground:
sentences.i: and for nine days, taking neither water nor food, she fed her fasting on nothing but dew and her own tears, and never moved from the ground.
sentences.n: 'luces' is 'lights' for 'days' — the same word family that has run through this whole tale of the Sun. Nine is the standing number for a stretch of grief or ritual in this poem. 'expers' takes the genitive ('undae… cibi'), 'having no part in.' 'ieiunia pavit' is a deliberate contradiction — she 'fed her fastings' — and 'rore mero' applies the wine-word 'merum' (unmixed) to dew, so that dew becomes the only drink she takes and is described as if it were a vintage.

sentences.t:
tantum spectabat euntis
ora dei vultusque suos flectebat ad illum.
sentences.l:
she only kept gazing at the face of the god as he went,
and kept turning her own face toward him.
sentences.i: She only watched the god's face as he travelled, and kept turning her own face after him.
sentences.n: Two imperfects, 'spectabat… flectebat,' for an action repeated all day and every day; the tense is what makes it a habit rather than an event. 'euntis' is the present participle of 'eo' in the genitive, agreeing with 'dei' — 'of the god as he goes' across the sky. 'ora' and 'vultus' are both plurals for singulars, and they are set against each other: his face and hers, one moving, one following. She is behaving like the flower before she is one.

sentences.t:
Membra ferunt haesisse solo, partemque coloris
luridus exsangues pallor convertit in herbas;
sentences.l:
Her limbs, they say, stuck fast to the ground, and part of her colour
a sallow paleness turned into bloodless plants;
sentences.i: Her limbs, they say, clung fast to the ground, and a sallow pallor turned part of her colouring into bloodless plants;
sentences.n: 'ferunt… haesisse' is 'they say that (her limbs) stuck' — the impersonal 'they say' Ovid uses to hold a transformation at arm's length, exactly as with 'fertur' at 245. 'exsangues' (bloodless) is the same word used of her rival's corpse at 244, now handed over to the growing thing she becomes ('herbae' is green stuff, not 'leaves'): the poem is quietly setting the two women's ends side by side. 'partem coloris' is 'part of her colour,' because the change is not complete — the next line keeps the red.

sentences.t:
est in parte rubor, violaeque simillimus ora
flos tegit.
sentences.l:
in part there is a redness, and a flower most like a violet
covers her face.
sentences.i: in part a redness stays, and a flower very like a violet covers her face.
sentences.n: 'simillimus' (most like) takes the dative 'violae.' 'ora' is the plain object of the active verb 'tegit,' a plural for a singular as at 265: the flower covers her face. It is not the Greek accusative of respect Ovid uses elsewhere for a body being altered — that idiom hangs on a passive or deponent participle, and 'tegit' has an object of its own. Ovid never names the plant; it is usually taken to be the heliotrope, the flower that follows the sun, and the violet is brought in only for the colour.

sentences.t:
Illa suum, quamvis radice tenetur,
vertitur ad Solem, mutataque servat amorem.”
sentences.l:
She, though she is held fast by a root,
turns toward her own Sun, and changed, keeps her love."
sentences.i: She, though held fast by a root, still turns to her own Sun; changed, she keeps her love."
sentences.n: 'suum' is cut off from 'Solem' by a whole clause — 'her own… Sun' — and the possessive is the point: he was never hers, and the poem goes on giving her the possessive to the end. 'vertitur' is passive in form and middle in force, 'turns herself.' 'mutata' is the poem's own word for its whole subject, and the last clause states the rule these tales run on: the shape goes, the passion stays. The closing quotation mark ends Leuconoe's story; another sister takes up the next.
